newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: S&P sees sound NZ fiscal outlook, c/a not a worry.
newsitem.headline: S&P sees sound NZ fiscal outlook, c/a not a worry.

text.p: A senior Standard and Poor's official said on Tuesday that New Zealand's current account deficit was not of concern provided the government kept running budget surpluses and paying off debt.

"If you're asking me if we're sitting here worrying about the current account deficit in the context of the credit rating of the government, the answer is no, we're not," S&P Sovereign Risk Managing Director David Beers said in a telephone interview.

"So long as the government is pursuing something like its current fiscal strategy, the exact level of the current account deficit...would not give rise to specific concerns on our part about the credit standing of the government."

S&P affirmed its AA+ foreign currency and AAA local currency ratings on New Zealand's long-term debt, together with its A-1+ short-term rating, after last October's election, which after tortuous negotiations produced a centre-right coalition.
Beers was asked to comment on remarks from Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash last week that the balance of payments deficit could not be sustained indefinitely.
He said he assumed Brash was commenting in the light of his long-stated preference for a lower exchange rate and higher interest rates.

"I suspect that he may be opining that it's unsustainable in the context of the exchange rate, but in our minds it doesn't raise larger credit implications for the government so long as their fiscal stance stays roughly in line with the present trajectory and they're actually reducing their indebtedness."

Asked if S&P was comfortable with the coalition government's plan for extra spending of $5 billion over three years, Beers said: "Provided that it's within the context of continuing to run a budget surplus, and if that proves to be sustainable."

He added: "Currently we see no signs that the fiscal policy is going to be blown out of the water. By that I mean a dramatic deterioration in the fiscal policy of the government, or reverting to a position of budget deficits. There's absolutely no sign of that happening."

Beers added: "The Reserve Bank is talking about monetary policy, which is not the same thing as the credit rating of the government. I would simply say that what they're talking about with respect to the exchange rate and with respect to the current account deficit is from a somewhat different perspective than we are."

New Zealand's current account deficit was NZ$4.2 billion in the year to September 1996, or 4.6 percent of GDP. The Reserve Bank forecast last week that it would peak at $6.17 billion on 5.9 percent of GDP in the year to March 1999.

Treasury this month forecast government operating surpluses of NZ$3.275 billion in 1997/98, $2.605 billion in 1998/99 and $3.457 billion in 1999/00. The latter is equivalent to 3.1 percent of GDP against the previous forecast of 5.5 pct.
Net public debt is seen falling to 17.8 percent of GDP by 1999/00 from 28.9 percent now.

Beers said S&P, at the time of its last upgrade of New Zealand in January 1996, did not assume budget surpluses would rise indefinitely. It took into account both the likelihood of tax cuts and the possibility of a change of government.

"What we were relying on, and continue to rely on, is a fiscal policy which continues to aim for budget surpluses going forward. And to the extent that that is realised, the rating remains secure at the present levels," he said.
Beers reiterated that the ratings outlook is stable. "What that means is that in a one to three-year timeframe we expect New Zealand's ratings to remain as they are."
